limitations_and_boundaries: No correlation between B. xylanisolvens abundance and NAFLD severity was observed in non-smokers.
The mechanisms of nicotine accumulation in the intestine need further study.
More research is needed to fully understand gut microbial nicotine-degrading ability.
The selected source chunks do not report a rescue, reconstitution, reversal, or epistasis experiment; that rung of the causal evidence chain remains untested within this extraction scope.

missed_core_items.description: The extraction omits the key result that nicotine concentrations in ileal content and tissue were higher in germ-free (GF) mice compared to SPF mice, indicating that endogenous gut bacteria contribute to nicotine degradation.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: In the nicotine drinking water delivery model, the nicotine concentrations in both the ileal content and ileal tissue in germ-free (GF) mice were higher than those in SPF mice, suggesting that endogenous gut bacteria contribute to nicotine degradation.

missed_core_items.description: The extraction omits the central finding that nicotine treatment induced phosphorylation of AMPKα at Thr172 in ileal organoids in a dose-dependent manner, which is a key mechanistic result.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: Consistent with previous studies21, we found that nicotine treatment induced the phosphorylation of AMPKα at Thr172 in ileal organoids in a dose-dependent manner (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b).

missed_core_items.description: The extraction omits the key result that B. xylanisolvens colonization inhibited nicotine-induced AMPKα phosphorylation in the ileum, which is a critical mechanistic link.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: B. xylanisolvens colonization inhibited nicotine-induced AMPKα phosphorylation in the ileum (Extended Data Fig. 4g).

missed_core_items.description: The extraction omits the key result that the loss of intestinal epithelial AMPKα1 improves hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis in the nicotine-accelerated NASH mouse model.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: Regarding the role of intestinal AMPKα1 in nicotine-accelerated NAFLD progression, we found that the loss of intestinal epithelial AMPKα1 contributes to improvements in hepatic steatosis, inflammation and fibrosis in the nicotine-accelerated NASH mouse model (Fig. 2b–f and Extended Data Fig. 5a–m).

missed_core_items.description: The extraction omits the key result that B. xylanisolvens-colonized SPF mice showed a reduction in ileal ceramides in the presence of NicX, which is a central finding linking bacterial degradation to ceramide reduction.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: In the nicotine-accelerated NASH mouse model, B. xylanisolvens-colonized SPF mice showed a reduction in ileal ceramides in the presence of NicX (Extended Data Fig. 7g), which resulted from the inhibition of the intestinal p-AMPKα–SMPD3 axis.

research_questions.statement: How does intestinal nicotine accumulation contribute to NAFLD progression, and can gut bacteria alleviate this effect?

provenance.text_excerpt: High levels of nicotine were detected in the ileal mucosa tissue of smokers, suggesting that nicotine accumulates in the intestine during tobacco smoking.

claims.statement: Nicotine accumulates in the intestine during tobacco smoking.

datasets.description: 30 non-smokers and 30 smokers with colon polyps; terminal ileum mucosa biopsy, serum, and stool samples collected.
datasets.name: Human cohort 1

datasets.description: SPF C57BL/6J mice given nicotine via smoke exposure, oral (drinking water), or subcutaneous injection.
datasets.name: Mouse nicotine administration models

experiments_or_tasks: Measurement of nicotine levels in ileal mucosa, serum, and stool from human smokers and non-smokers.
Measurement of nicotine levels in various tissues of SPF mice after smoke exposure, oral, or subcutaneous nicotine administration.

methods.name: LC-MS/MS nicotine quantification
methods.protocol_description: Nicotine and HPB measured by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Tissue samples homogenized, extracted with ethyl acetate, analyzed using QTRAP 5500 with Waters XBridge amide column.

study_units.name: Nicotine accumulation in intestine

results.metric_name: Nicotine concentration in ileal content and tissue

provenance.text_excerpt: Ileal nicotine accumulation was consistently observed in the above mouse models (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1a).

results.value_raw_text: Ileal nicotine accumulation was consistently observed in mouse models (smoke exposure, oral, subcutaneous).

provenance.text_excerpt: High levels of nicotine were detected in the ileal mucosa tissue of smokers, suggesting that nicotine accumulates in the intestine during tobacco smoking (Fig. 1a).

results.value_raw_text: High levels of nicotine were detected in the ileal mucosa tissue of smokers.

provenance.text_excerpt: In smokers, B. xylanisolvens abundance was negatively correlated with faecal nicotine content, but positively correlated with HPB levels (Fig. 4e,f).

claims.statement: B. xylanisolvens abundance is negatively correlated with NAFLD severity and faecal nicotine, and positively correlated with HPB levels in smokers.

provenance.text_excerpt: these data establish intestinal nicotine accumulation as a risk factor for clinical NAFLD progression in smokers, while also suggesting that B. xylanisolvens, with its nicotine-degrading activities, could exhibit protective effects by decreasing the progression of NAFLD (Extended Data Fig. 10k).

claims.statement: Intestinal nicotine accumulation is a risk factor for NAFLD progression in smokers, and B. xylanisolvens may protect against NAFLD progression by degrading nicotine.

datasets.description: 83 patients with biopsy-proven NAFLD: 41 smokers (cohort 2) and 42 non-smokers (cohort 3). Serum and stool samples collected.
datasets.name: Human cohort 2 and 3

experiments_or_tasks: Analysis of B. xylanisolvens abundance, faecal nicotine, HPB, and serum ceramides in 83 patients with biopsy-proven NAFLD (smokers and non-smokers).

methods.name: Metagenomic sequencing
methods.protocol_description: DNA extracted from stool samples, libraries prepared using Ultra DNA Library Prep Kit, sequenced.

study_units.name: Clinical correlation of B. xylanisolvens with NAFLD

provenance.text_excerpt: the faecal nicotine levels were step-wise increased with the progression of NAFLD, and the nicotine-degradation product HPB in faeces was accordingly decreased along with NAFLD progression (Fig. 4c,d).

results.value_raw_text: Faecal nicotine levels increased step-wise with NAFLD progression; HPB decreased.

provenance.text_excerpt: The serum ceramide levels, especially ceramide (d18:1/16:0), which is mainly derived from the intestine, were significantly higher in individuals with NASH compared with those with NAFL (Fig. 4h), and it was negatively correlated with the abundance of B. xylanisolvens (Fig. 4i).

results.value_raw_text: Serum ceramide (d18:1/16:0) levels were significantly higher in NASH compared with NAFL, and negatively correlated with B. xylanisolvens abundance.

results.metric_name: B. xylanisolvens abundance vs NAFLD severity

provenance.text_excerpt: we found that B. xylanisolvens levels were negatively correlated with NAFLD severity (that is, from NAFL to borderline NASH to definite NASH), as indicated by the NAFLD-activity score (NAS) (Fig. 4a,b and Extended Data Fig. 10a–c).

results.value_raw_text: B. xylanisolvens levels were negatively correlated with NAFLD severity (NAS score) in smokers.

provenance.text_excerpt: We identify the gut bacterium Bacteroides xylanisolvens as an effective nicotine degrader.

claims.statement: Bacteroides xylanisolvens degrades nicotine in the gut and reduces intestinal nicotine levels.

experiments_or_tasks: Colonization of B. xylanisolvens in nicotine-exposed mice reduces intestinal nicotine concentrations.
Identification of B. xylanisolvens as an effective nicotine degrader.

methods.name: Bacterial colonization
methods.protocol_description: SPF mice gavaged with 2×10^8 CFU of B. xylanisolvens or nicX-knockout B. xylanisolvens in 200 μl anaerobic PBS every 3 days.

study_units.name: Bacteroides xylanisolvens degrades nicotine

provenance.text_excerpt: Colonization of B. xylanisolvens reduces intestinal nicotine concentrations in nicotine-exposed mice, and it improves nicotine-exacerbated NAFLD progression.

results.value_raw_text: Colonization of B. xylanisolvens reduces intestinal nicotine concentrations in nicotine-exposed mice.

provenance.text_excerpt: AMPKα promotes the phosphorylation of sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3 (SMPD3), stabilizing the latter and therefore increasing intestinal ceramide formation, which contributes to NAFLD progression to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).

claims.statement: Nicotine activates intestinal AMPKα, which phosphorylates and stabilizes SMPD3, increasing ceramide production and promoting NAFLD progression.

experiments_or_tasks: Demonstration that nicotine activates intestinal AMPKα, which phosphorylates and stabilizes SMPD3, increasing ceramide production.
In vitro kinase assays showing AMPKα phosphorylates SMPD3.
In vivo ceramide supplementation and GW4869 treatment in mice.
Organoid experiments with AMPK inhibitor compound C and SMPD3 overexpression.

methods.name: In vitro kinase assay
methods.protocol_description: Bacterially purified SMPD3-His (86-655) proteins incubated with active AMPK heterotrimer and [γ-32P]ATP at 30°C for 2 h; reaction stopped by SDS sample buffer, resolved by SDS-PAGE, autoradiography.

methods.name: Ileal organoid culture and treatment
methods.protocol_description: Ileal crypts isolated from mice, cultured in Matrigel and IntestiCult medium. Treated with nicotine (1 μg/ml), compound C (20 μM), GW4869 (10 μM), or lentiviral SMPD3 overexpression.

study_units.name: Mechanism: AMPKα-SMPD3-ceramide axis

provenance.text_excerpt: SMPD3 overexpression reversed the reduction in ceramide levels resulting from AMPKα1 deficiency in ileal organoids (Extended Data Fig. 7e,f).

results.value_raw_text: SMPD3 overexpression reversed the reduction in ceramide levels resulting from AMPKα1 deficiency in ileal organoids.

provenance.text_excerpt: The protective effects on hepatic steatosis, inflammation and fibrosis resulting from the genetic disruption of intestinal epithelium AMPKα1 were reversed by ceramide (d18:1/16:0) administration (Extended Data Fig. 8b–s).

results.value_raw_text: Ceramide (d18:1/16:0) administration reversed the protective effects of intestinal AMPKα1 deficiency on hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis.

provenance.text_excerpt: The ceramide levels in organoids and their supernatants under nicotine treatment were decreased by GW4869 (Extended Data Fig. 7b,c).

results.value_raw_text: Nicotine treatment increased ceramide levels in organoids; compound C (AMPK inhibitor) decreased ceramide levels.

provenance.text_excerpt: oral GW4869 delivery decreased the ileal levels of ceramides, and the decrease was accompanied by lower NAFLD severity in the nicotine-drinking model (Extended Data Fig. 9a–s).

results.value_raw_text: Oral GW4869 decreased ileal ceramides and reduced NAFLD severity in nicotine-drinking mice.
